ARM.text:
Nvidia's headhunters approached Arm CEO Rene Haas to run the chipmaker. Masayoshi Son just promoted him instead.

Haas signed a new deal today to stay at Arm through 2033 and become SoftBank's Vice Chairman on December 1. Arm shares jumped over 10% in premarket trading.

Nvidia's board is still hunting for a permanent CEO after founder Jensen Huang stepped down earlier this month. Its stock bounced over 8% premarket today after Trump urged the board to rehire Huang.

Rene Haas kept his commercial freedom under Son. Nvidia's board still doesn't have a CEO.
ARM.note: Why Arm moved: Nvidia's recruiters approached Haas; SoftBank locked him in through 2033 and made him vice chair.

ARM.name: Desiree
ARM.text:
SoftBank just took away Nvidia's safest excuse not to call Jensen Huang back, and President Trump just handed shareholders the permission slip to demand it.

​Nvidia's search firm went after Arm CEO Rene Haas to replace Huang, so Masayoshi Son wrote a golden-handcuffs check through 2033 to lock the top outside candidate in the building. 

That leaves Nvidia's board trapped between a massive stock slide and no clean external replacement.

​Meanwhile, Trump publicly urging Nvidia to reinstate Huang removes the biggest political fear holding the board back.

Does Nvidia cave?
ARM.note: Connects the SoftBank/Haas move to the Huang reinstatement.

SOXX.name: Michael Fridman
SOXX.text:
5 TMT takeaways from last week:

1/ The Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4%, its worst week since March 2020. Semis lost ~17%, and the S&P 500 dropped 8.6%, ending roughly 12% below its October high after seven consecutive down sessions. Tech has seen aggressive rotation for six months, but Friday felt different, perhaps the first session that smelled like panic. The VIX touched 40 before cooling to around 36 late in the session. Some of the volatility bid appeared exhausted into the close, which could help a temporary bounce. But strong $NVDA results and a massive Anthropic IPO failed to restore confidence. Investors are questioning who finances the next round of AI spending, what returns it earns and whether earnings estimates hold. With the 10-year near 5% and further Fed tightening in focus, selling spread beyond AI into broader growth concerns. The market feels increasingly bear-ish, even without a formal 20% index drawdown.

2/ $NVDA doubled revenue to $115.8B and guided the next quarter to $130B. Demand was not the weak point. The CEO search, a 10-Q still to come and reports of an SEC accounting investigation left other questions open. The board also faces a difficult appointment: if the investigation establishes wrongdoing, an internal successor could leave doubts about whether enough has changed. If it does not, refusing to reconsider Jensen would be a mistake. I think the stock could remain in the penalty box under either scenario, despite strong operating results. For the stock to get back to grace, and perhpas even the market, Jensen getting re-instated seems to be the right path.

3/ $ANT public offering reached $93.5B gross, including secondary shares, alongside a $26B private placement. Even that failed to settle the funding debate. Consensus forecasts put cloud provider cash burn at ~$361B in 2027, versus ~$140B this year. Nvidia is also becoming more selective about customer financing commitments. Capital remains available, but its cost and conditions matter more. I would distinguish projects with secured financing, tenants and power from those still depending on all three coming together.

4/ Positioning and thin liquidity amplified the move. Single stock shorting was the heaviest since June 2022, ETF shorts rose 11%, and market depth was near the year’s low. That helps explain the speed of the decline. It does not prove everyone has sold: systematic exposure was low, but broader positioning remained above average. Friday showed signs of panic; I am less convinced we have seen enough selling across investor groups to call a durable bottom.

5/ $PANW was a standout, as I discussed in a separate post: $630M of net new next-generation security ARR and a higher full-year outlook. $KEYS  orders rose 53%, while Lenovo’s GPU-server revenue grew more than 300%. There is no uniform collapse in operating demand. My concern is that financing costs, lower project returns and approval delays eventually change future spending plans. The selloff may not be over; sideways trading is also possible. Beyond a temporary bounce, I still do not see enough catalysts for a meaningful, sustained rally. I would keep the hedges on and add selectively.
